source.version: Journal version of record: Journal of Innovation & Knowledge 12 (2026) 100892; received 1 July 2025, accepted 11 November 2025, available online 17 November 2025 (p. 1, header and footer). The retrieval record marks it as the latest version.
source.title_on_document: AI as a cognitive collaborator: Assimilation and accommodation in human–machine teaming for innovation

supplement.where: No external supplementary material or online appendix is referenced. The article's Appendix A (survey instruments and measurement details) is included in this PDF on p. 10 and is referenced on p. 6, Measures.
supplement.holds: Appendix A lists survey items for pre-task controls, cognitive strategy, emotional engagement, perceived performance, and technology acceptance; it contains no arm-contrast statistics. The supplementary robustness analyses treating accommodation as continuous are described as consistent with the main findings, but no numerical results or external location are supplied (p. 5, Measures).

paper_design_summary: The study recruited 371 mid-career professionals in South Korea for a 2 x 2 experiment using stratified randomization of GPT-4 availability and individual versus dyad work; the allocation unit and total analyzed headcount are not unambiguously reported (p. 1, Abstract; p. 5, Procedures). Participants completed a 90-minute open-ended innovation challenge in a controlled virtual environment; AI conditions first received a 45-minute prompt-engineering and GPT-4 training module, while any matched control activity is not described (p. 5, Procedures). Blind expert raters scored solution quality, novelty, and feasibility on a 10-point scale, and experts rated technical/commercial integration on a 1-7 balance index (pp. 5-6, Measures).

studies.label: 2 x 2 factorial experiment (GenAI vs no GenAI x individual vs dyad), innovation challenge

assignment.what_was_assigned: GenAI availability (GPT-4 with a 45-minute prompt-engineering training module versus no AI) crossed with collaboration structure (alone versus dyad). The allocation unit and when or how dyads were formed are not stated (p. 5, Procedures).
assignment.quote: Importantly, conditions were assigned using a stratified randomization procedure accounting for prior AI exposure, job function, and digital fluency.
assignment.locator: p. 5, Methodology, Procedures; p. 1, Abstract (randomized 2 × 2 factorial field experiment)

participants.exclusions: Exclusions, attrition, and counts at assignment are not stated. The paper reports 371 recruited professionals (p. 5, Procedures). Table 2 reports Individual No AI N = 92 and Individual AI N = 90, supporting those analyzed person counts (p. 6). The Team No AI N = 95 and Team AI N = 94 entries do not define their counting unit, and the odd Team No AI count is unexplained given the stated dyads. The four printed Ns sum to the recruitment count, but this does not establish a final analyzed headcount or zero exclusions. Team-arm and total analyzed person counts are therefore null; counts_are denotes people in the retained participant-count fields, not a claim that the team table entries count people. Table 3 provides no regression N (p. 6); Appendix A supplies no participant-flow clarification (p. 10).

ai_tool.how_used: Participants in the AI conditions took a 45-minute training module on prompt engineering and hands-on interaction with GPT-4, then could use GPT-4 during the 90-minute problem-solving phase. Their prompt histories were analyzed with the submitted solutions (p. 5, Procedures and Measures; p. 7, prompts such as 'Refine my draft' and 'What if customers contributed their own designs?'). The paper does not describe training or any matched activity for the no-AI arms (p. 5, Procedures).

task.description: Open-ended innovation challenge meant to mirror real organizational problems, e.g., developing a novel digital product, reimagining customer service processes, or integrating sustainability principles into an existing offering (p. 5)
task.duration: 90-minute problem-solving phase (plus a 45-minute training module for the AI arms)

outcomes.name: Solution quality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Independent expert raters, blind to condition and identity, scored each solution on a 10-point Likert scale adapted from Dell'Acqua et al. (2025); inter-rater reliability ICC2 = 0.51 (p. 5, Measures). The number of raters is not stated. Analyzed with OLS regression and two-way ANOVA, with controls such as gender, role, and prior AI experience 'where relevant' (p. 6). Table 3 prints no regression N and does not say whether the coefficients are standardized. Experts rated submitted solutions, but the paper does not explain whether a dyad solution contributes one observation per team, one per member, or another aggregation to the descriptive and regression analyses. The analysis unit is therefore unconfirmed and coded null (p. 5, Procedures and Measures; p. 6, Data analysis strategy and Tables 2-3).

eligibility.reason: GenAI availability versus no AI was explicitly assigned using stratified randomization, crossed with individual versus dyad work on an open-ended innovation challenge (p. 5, Procedures; p. 1, Abstract). The allocation unit is unspecified, but random assignment of AI access is explicit. The two individual arms have 90 and 92 analyzed people in Table 2; 90 + 92 = 182, which exceeds 50 without relying on the ambiguous team-row Ns (p. 6, Table 2). The reported 371 is a recruitment count; the total analyzed headcount is unconfirmed (p. 5, Procedures). Independent experts rated each produced solution for quality, novelty, and feasibility, blind to condition and identity; GPT-4 was available during production in the AI arms (p. 5, Procedures and Measures; p. 7, illustrative prompt histories). Unreported control activities, dyad observation units, and inconsistencies among the regression and summary tables affect extraction and interpretation, not these eligibility determinations.

one_line_finding: Among analyzed individual participants (90 with GPT-4, 92 without AI), the AI arm had higher expert-rated solution novelty (7.1 vs 5.8) and quality (7.3 vs 6.2) on 10-point scales (p. 6, Table 2; p. 5, Measures).
open_questions: Participants worked alone or in dyads (p. 5, Procedures), but Table 2 lists Team No AI N = 95 and Team AI N = 94 without defining whether these are people or dyads (p. 6). The odd Team No AI count and mapping of team solutions to observations are unexplained. All four outcome unit fields and team-arm analyzed person counts are null; clarify team membership, rating aggregation, and regression rows before team-effect extraction.

The relation between Table 3 coefficients and Table 2 means is not explained. For quality, means are 7.3 vs 6.2 in the individual arms and 7.5 vs 6.5 in the team arms, while Table 3 reports GenAI β = .41 and GenAI × Team β = .58 (p < 0.001). Outcome/coefficient standardization, exact adjustment specifications, and regression N are not given (p. 6, Data analysis strategy and Tables 2-3).

Table 3 labels a row 'GenAI × Team', but the text describes teams using GenAI as achieving the strongest results overall (β = 0.58, p < .001). The model coding/reference group and a direct Team AI versus Team No AI regression contrast are not supplied (p. 6, Table 3 and Results); no such direct contrast is inferred.

Table 6 cites 'Team effect: β = 0.336, p < .001' for H1–2 (p. 8), whereas Table 3 reports Collaboration (team) β = .11, n.s., and the Results text says teams without GenAI did not outperform individuals without it (p. 6). The source does not identify an alternative model or contrast explaining the difference.

The AI arms received a 45-minute prompt-engineering and GPT-4 training module before the task (p. 5, Procedures). What the no-AI arms did during that interval is not stated; an absence of matched training or activity cannot be asserted. Clarification is needed to separate the contribution of training from access to GPT-4.

The number of independent expert raters and the details of rating aggregation are not stated; ICC2 = 0.51 is reported for quality, novelty, and feasibility (p. 5, Measures). Expert scoring of the solutions is explicit regardless of the unreported rater count.

The paper calls the study a field experiment (p. 1, Abstract), but describes a controlled virtual environment and simulated workplace conditions (p. 5, Procedures). Retain lab_rct as the screening classification for this controlled task; this subclassification does not change the explicit randomization or eligibility.

The unit of randomization and how or when dyads were formed are not stated (p. 5, Procedures). Stratification used prior AI exposure, job function, and digital fluency, but these traits do not establish the allocation unit. assignment.unit is null pending clarification; randomized remains yes.

The paper reports 371 recruited professionals but no counts at assignment, exclusions, attrition, or regression N (pp. 5-6, Procedures, Data analysis strategy and Tables 2-3). The total analyzed headcount is null because the team Ns have an unspecified unit. The individual arms' 90 and 92 analyzed people independently meet the size criterion.
notes: Outcomes listed are the four expert-rated solution outcomes in Tables 2 and 3. Not listed because they are self-reported or not scored on the output: change in positive and negative emotion (pre-post self-reports on a 7-point scale, Table 2), the assimilation vs accommodation classification (survey items plus coded prompt histories, solutions, and interviews), perceived performance, and technology acceptance (Appendix A). Table 4 (p. 7, mediation by accommodation; for novelty, direct effect of GenAI .32, indirect effect .19, 37 percent mediated, bootstrapped 95 percent CI [.10, 0.28]) and Table 5 (p. 8, moderated mediation by emotional engagement) are mechanism analyses, not arm contrasts. No overall creativity rating and no diversity measure across people are reported. Quality and feasibility are coded usefulness under the codebook. The paper names no primary outcome. Under codebook rule 2 for with_ai, expert-rated novelty (S1-O2) is the first available construct, and its individual-arm contrast is the one with a regression coefficient and SE. The two raw forms agreed on design, counts, outcomes, constructs, and every Table 2 and Table 3 number they both recorded; the reconciliation settled the supplement coding, the AI-availability code, and B's fuller copy of Table 3. Final review checked the complete markdown including Appendix A and the PDF passages and tables underlying the recorded numbers. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as a historical record; its inferred individual allocation unit and total/team analyzed headcounts are superseded by the finalized fields and challenge resolutions. No effect sizes were computed. Remaining reporting questions are classified in final.open_items; none prevents core eligibility.

open_items.item: Open question 1: team-row counting units and aggregation of dyad solutions (pp. 5-6). Authors must identify people, dyads, and analysis rows and explain the odd Team No AI N. This affects extraction; individual-arm counts already exceed 50 and solution scoring is explicit.

Open question 2: regression scaling, adjustments, model N, and relationship to descriptive means (p. 6, Tables 2-3). Authors must supply model specifications or analysis data/code. This concerns effect estimation, not randomization, the size threshold, or output scoring.

Open question 3: interpretation of the GenAI x Team row and direct team AI versus no-AI contrast (p. 6, Table 3 and Results). Authors must specify model coding and the intended contrast. This affects the estimate to extract, not eligibility.

Open question 4: Table 6 team coefficient versus Table 3 and Results (pp. 6, 8). Authors must identify the underlying model/contrast or correct the inconsistent reporting. This affects result interpretation, not the three eligibility criteria.

Open question 5: no-AI training or matched activity during the AI training interval (p. 5, Procedures). Authors must provide the control protocol. AI availability was explicitly randomized, so this concerns intervention interpretation rather than eligibility.

Open question 6: expert-rater count and rating aggregation (p. 5, Measures). Authors must provide the rater roster/count and aggregation procedure. Expert scoring of produced solutions is already explicit, so criterion 3 is met.

Open question 7: randomized-design subclass (p. 1, Abstract; p. 5, Procedures). Retain lab_rct for the described controlled virtual task and simulated workplace setting. This coding choice does not alter random assignment of AI; nothing further is needed for screening eligibility.

Open question 8: allocation unit and dyad-formation sequence (p. 5, Procedures). Authors must provide the assignment protocol. Stratified random assignment of AI availability is explicit, so the unspecified unit does not prevent criterion 1 from being met.

Open question 9: assignment counts, exclusions/attrition, and total analyzed headcount (pp. 5-6; Appendix A, p. 10). Authors must provide participant flow and analysis-specific counts. The 90 and 92 analyzed people in the individual arms already meet criterion 2.
